lead.kicker: TOP STORY  •  THE GULF WAR WIDENS
lead.headline: Strike on Riyadh's Airport Pulls Saudi Arabia Deeper Into Yemen's War
lead.deck: At least 12 people were killed at the Saudi capital's main airport. President Trump says the US may join the fight against the Iran-backed Houthis.
body: Yemen's war reached the heart of Saudi Arabia on Saturday. An attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, the capital, killed at least 12 people and injured 309, the Saudi aviation authority said. Two days earlier a missile strike on the same airport had killed three Saudis, one of them a pilot.

The likely attackers are the Houthis, an Iran-backed movement that has ruled northern Yemen since 2014. They claimed Thursday's strike and told airlines to avoid Saudi airspace. Their missiles answer an offensive that Yemen's Saudi-backed government launched on October 4 to retake Houthi territory, supported by Saudi-led air strikes on Sanaa, the Houthi-held capital.

The fighting is now tangled up with the wider US-Iran war. Asked whether the United States would join the Saudis, President Trump said: "We may. We're going to look at it." At a rally in New York on Friday he said he was "about to settle, or win" the war with Iran. The UN's envoy for Yemen warned that the country has slid back into full-scale war.

map.title: BAB EL-MANDEB, THE GATE OF TEARS
map.footnote: About 30 km of water at its narrowest point
map.caption: With Hormuz disrupted, Saudi oil now leaves through this strait.

lead.why: This is where a local war meets the world economy. Iran's war with the US has choked the Strait of Hormuz: crude exports through it fell to about 8.5 million barrels a day in the week to October 7, roughly 40% below pre-war levels. Saudi Arabia has rerouted oil west to the Red Sea, which can only be reached through the Bab el-Mandeb, beside Yemen. In September the Houthis seized the coast along it. If they can threaten that last exit, Iran gains leverage without firing at Saudi Arabia itself.
lead.analyst: Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, closed near $104.50 a barrel on Friday, about two-thirds higher than a year ago but slightly lower than a month ago. Why might prices fall while the fighting spreads? Consider what traders may already have expected, and what would move prices sharply from here.

world.headline: Pillay's Nobel Collides With a US Assault on the World's War-Crimes Court
world.deck: The Norwegian committee honoured a judge who built international criminal law. Washington sanctioned her old court the same day.
body: Navi Pillay, 85, was born in Durban in 1941, the daughter of a bus driver, under South Africa's apartheid laws. As a lawyer she fought them; as a judge she helped convict people for the 1994 Rwandan genocide, sat on the International Criminal Court (ICC) from 2003 to 2008, and served as the UN's human rights chief. On Friday she won the Nobel Peace Prize.

The choice is contested. A UN commission she led concluded last year that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza, a finding Israel rejects as biased. Prime Minister Netanyahu said the committee had "lost its moral compass". President Trump said the United States "should have received" the prize and called Pillay someone "nobody has ever heard of".

Hours after the award, the US sanctioned the ICC as an institution, not only its officials, cutting it off from US transactions. Washington cites the court's Afghanistan investigation, which could reach US personnel, and its arrest warrants for Netanyahu and his former defence minister. The court called it an "assault on the rule of law"; the UN secretary-general called it a serious blow.

Pillay herself answered with humour. She said she first thought the call "must be a joke", told an audience she might share the prize with Trump if they clapped a little more, and dedicated it to all the survivors of international crimes. Japan's prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, a close US ally, said she was deeply concerned by the sanctions.

The fight is also in American courts. In August, Human Rights Watch sued in US federal court to have the earlier sanctions on ICC officials struck down; the new measures widen the target to any company that does business with the court.

illustration.title: THE PEACE PRIZE
illustration.subtitle: Oslo, Norway
illustration.caption: Pillay sat as an ICC judge from 2003 to 2008. The court has 125 member states.

world.connect: Pillay's life links two struggles over who answers to the law. Apartheid was legal: South Africa's parliament wrote it down. Activists like Nelson Mandela, whose release Pillay campaigned for, argued that a law can itself be unjust. International criminal courts rest on a related idea: that some acts are crimes even when a government orders them. The US, Russia, China and Israel have never accepted the ICC's authority over their citizens, which is the heart of today's clash.

us.headline: Trump Strikes a Diesel Deal With Putin, Weeks After Sanctioning Him
us.deck: Russia will sell diesel into US and global markets under a sanctions waiver. Ukraine says the deal rewards Moscow without a ceasefire.
body: Diesel powers the trucks, trains, farm machines and ships that move almost everything, and the Gulf war has made it scarce. On Friday President Trump announced that Russia would supply more than 300,000 tons immediately, 500,000 tons in November and a million tons after that.

To make it legal, the Treasury issued a licence waiving sanctions on Russian diesel until April 2027, only weeks after Trump signed sweeping new sanctions on Russia. The Kremlin said the deal would benefit the global economy.

Ukraine's President Zelensky condemned it, warning that easing sanctions without a Russian commitment to de-escalate will only prolong the war. The deal landed while Trump's envoys were meeting Ukrainian officials in Miami to discuss a peace proposal.
us.why: Sanctions work by cutting an economy off from customers; Russia earns much of its money selling fuel. Lifting even part of them is leverage the US can only spend once, and it changes what Russia gains by talking peace.
us.analyst: Supporters say cheaper diesel helps American families before the November 3 midterms; critics say it funds Russia's war. One Atlantic Council analyst called the volumes uncertain and too small to end the shortage. What evidence would settle it?
also: Hurricane Isaias hit Florida's Panhandle as a Category 2 storm, killing at least four people and cutting power to more than 858,000 homes and businesses.
SpaceX agreed to buy low-band airwaves for about $8 billion for its Starlink phone service, and AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile shares fell.

uk.headline: Burnham Moves to Curb the Clauses That Stop Workers Switching Jobs
uk.deck: About 5 million employees in Great Britain have contracts that bar them from joining a rival. The government says it will legislate.
body: A non-compete clause is a promise in a job contract: if you leave, you will not work for a competitor for a set period. Employers say they protect trade secrets and clients. Critics say they trap workers and starve new companies of talent.

The government estimates that about 5 million employees in Great Britain have one, typically lasting about six months. Prime Minister Andy Burnham says he will legislate so that they are no longer a barrier to hiring for promising start-ups. Long notice periods are also in his sights. He presented the change as a way to help young firms grow.

No bill has been published, and it is not yet clear whether the clauses will be banned or capped. In 2023 the previous government planned a three-month limit that never became law. Details may come in the Budget on October 28.

chart.title: HOW LONG A NON-COMPETE LASTS
chart.subtitle: Months a worker is barred from a rival
chart.caption: The 2023 plan was never passed. No new limit has been set yet.

uk.why: Economies grow when skills move to where they are most useful. If millions of workers cannot change jobs within their field, wages and new businesses can both suffer.
uk.analyst: In English law a non-compete is already unenforceable unless an employer can show it is reasonable. So how much does a clause matter if a court might strike it down? Think about how many workers would risk a lawsuit to find out.

items: Panama: a magnitude 7.7 earthquake injured 27 people and damaged more than 400 homes; the government declared a state of emergency.
EU and China: Beijing agreed to cut hybrid car exports to Europe by more than half over four years, the EU's trade chief said.

items.def: A conflict in which a power arms another group to fight for it. Today: Iran-backed Houthis against Saudi Arabia.
The authority of a court over people or places. Today: the US rejects the ICC's jurisdiction over Americans.
An official decision to set a rule aside. Today: a Treasury waiver lets Russian diesel be sold until April 2027.
A contract clause barring a worker from joining a rival. Today: about 5 million British workers have one.

did_you_know.text: Diesel fuel is named after Rudolf Diesel, a German engineer who demonstrated his engine in 1897. It ignites fuel using only the heat of tightly squeezed air, with no spark plug, which is why diesel engines are so efficient at hauling heavy loads.

sports.title: Ronaldo suspended by his own country
sports.body: Cristiano Ronaldo, Portugal's 41-year-old captain, has been provisionally suspended by the Portuguese Football Federation, which opened a disciplinary case on Friday. He walked out of the team's camp in Copenhagen on September 30 after a dispute with coach Jorge Jesus. The rules allow a ban of one to six months.
